title: The mole and molar mass
summary: Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in [[mole|moles]]. One mole is about $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles, the number set by the [[avogadro-constant|Avogadro constant]]. The [[molar-mass|molar mass]] turns that count into a mass you can weigh, through $n = \frac{m}{M}$.

goals.text: Convert between an amount in moles and a number of atoms, molecules, [[ion|ions]] or electrons, using the Avogadro constant.
Explain what relative atomic mass and [[relative-formula-mass|relative formula mass]] compare, and why they have no units.
Calculate $M_\text{r}$ for any formula, including ionic compounds and hydrates, from the data booklet's $A_\text{r}$ values.
Solve problems linking mass, amount in moles and number of particles, using $n = \frac{m}{M}$ with $M$ in $\pu{g mol-1}$.

before.prompt: Which of these substances is an [[element|element]]?
before.hint: An element contains atoms of only one kind, even if they are joined together.
before.explain: Oxygen gas, $\ce{O2}$, contains only oxygen atoms, joined in pairs. The other three each contain two elements bonded together, so they are [[compound|compounds]]. Revise it in {{lesson:1.1}}.

before.prompt: Chlorine has two [[isotope|isotopes]], chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Why is its [[relative-atomic-mass|relative atomic mass]] not a whole number?
before.hint: A sample of chlorine is a mixture of both isotopes.

options.text: It is a weighted mean of the isotope masses, based on their abundances.
Chlorine atoms contain a fraction of a neutron.
It is the simple average of the two mass numbers.
Chlorine-37 is the more common isotope.

before.explain: Each isotope has a whole number of protons and [[neutron|neutrons]]. A natural sample holds about three chlorine-35 atoms for every chlorine-37 atom, so the weighted mean lies between 35 and 37, nearer 35. Revise it in {{lesson:1.2}}.

verify.truth: It is a weighted mean of the isotope masses, based on their abundances.

before.prompt: How many atoms are in one formula unit of magnesium hydroxide, $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$?
before.hint: The 2 after the bracket multiplies everything inside it.
before.explain: One magnesium, two oxygens and two hydrogens: $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ atoms. Revise it in {{lesson:1.1}}.

blocks.text: Atoms and molecules are tiny. One drop of water holds about $2 \times 10^{21}$ molecules, far too many to count one at a time.
So chemists count particles in fixed bundles, the way shops sell eggs by the dozen. The chemist's bundle is the mole, symbol $\text{mol}$. It is huge, because particles are so small.

blocks.statement: The unit of amount of substance, $n$, in the SI system. A mole of any substance holds exactly $N_\text{A}$ elementary entities, where $N_\text{A}$ is the Avogadro constant.
blocks.plain: A mole is a count, like a dozen, but of about 602 thousand billion billion particles.

blocks.text: The data booklet (section 2) gives $N_\text{A} = \pu{6.02e23 mol-1}$. The unit $\pu{mol-1}$ reads "per mole": there are $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles in every mole.
Amount of substance is a count of particles. It is not a mass and not a volume, even though you will often work it out from one.
Always say what you are counting. The counted particle, the elementary entity, can be atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, or a fixed group such as one formula unit of $\ce{NaCl}$.
Here $N$ is the number of particles and $n$ is the amount in moles. To go the other way, divide: $n = \frac{N}{N_\text{A}}$.

One mole of molecules can hold several moles of atoms. One mole of $\ce{H2O}$ holds $\pu{2 mol}$ of hydrogen atoms and $\pu{1 mol}$ of oxygen atoms. Multiply by how many of that particle one formula contains.

blocks.question: A balloon holds $\pu{0.0450 mol}$ of carbon dioxide, $\ce{CO2}$. Calculate the number of $\ce{CO2}$ molecules, using section 2 of the data booklet.
steps: The particle is the $\ce{CO2}$ molecule, so use $N = n \times N_\text{A}$ directly.
Round to 3 significant figures, matching $0.0450$.

blocks.question: Calculate the total number of ions in $\pu{0.0160 mol}$ of aluminium sulfate, $\ce{Al2(SO4)3}$.
steps: Count the ions in one formula unit: two $\ce{Al^3+}$ and three $\ce{SO4^2-}$, so five ions.
Amount of ions: $n = 5 \times 0.0160 = \pu{0.0800 mol}$.
$N = 0.0800 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 4.816 \times 10^{22}$, which rounds to 3 significant figures.
Sense check: five ions per unit, so the answer is five times the number of formula units.

blocks.text: Using the amount of the compound when the question asks about one kind of particle. One mole of $\ce{Al2(SO4)3}$ holds $\pu{2 mol}$ of $\ce{Al^3+}$ and $\pu{5 mol}$ of ions in total.

blocks.prompt: A sample of neon contains $1.505 \times 10^{24}$ atoms. What amount of neon is this, in mol? Give 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Going from particles to moles, divide by $N_\text{A}$.

blocks.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in $\pu{0.500 mol}$ of sulfur trioxide, $\ce{SO3}$?
blocks.hint: First find the amount of oxygen atoms, then multiply by $N_\text{A}$.
blocks.explain: Each $\ce{SO3}$ has three oxygen atoms, so there are $3 \times 0.500 = \pu{1.50 mol}$ of them. $1.50 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 9.03 \times 10^{23}$. The other options forget the 3, count all four atoms, or stop at moles.

blocks.text: One carbon-12 atom has a mass of about $\pu{2e-23 g}$. Numbers that small are awkward, so chemists compare the masses of atoms with each other instead.
The standard is the carbon-12 atom, $\ce{^{12}C}$, given a mass of exactly 12 on this scale. One-twelfth of its mass is the unit every other atom is measured against.

Relative atomic mass, $A_\text{r}$, is the weighted mean mass of an element's atoms on that scale. Use the values in section 7 of the data booklet, to two decimal places: $\ce{H}$ $1.01$, $\ce{C}$ $12.01$, $\ce{O}$ $16.00$.
Carbon's $A_\text{r}$ is $12.01$, not 12, because natural carbon contains a little carbon-13.

blocks.statement: $M_\text{r}$: the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a formula, on the scale where one carbon-12 atom has a mass of exactly 12.
blocks.plain: How heavy one formula unit is compared with one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.

blocks.why: Each is a mass divided by a mass (one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom), so the units cancel.

blocks.text: $M_\text{r}$ works for every formula. That includes ionic compounds such as $\ce{NaCl}$, which are lattices of ions, not molecules. For them, the formula describes one formula unit.

To find $M_\text{r}$, count the atoms of each element, multiply each count by its $A_\text{r}$, then add. A bracket multiplies everything inside it. In a hydrate, the dot means "plus": add the water molecules too.
Atoms generally get heavier as atomic number rises, with a few exceptions such as argon and potassium. Down a group, each atom has more protons and neutrons than the one above, so $A_\text{r}$ rises.

blocks.question: Determine the relative formula mass of copper(II) nitrate, $\ce{Cu(NO3)2}$, using section 7 of the data booklet.
steps: Count the atoms. The bracket doubles $\ce{NO3}$: one $\ce{Cu}$, two $\ce{N}$ and six $\ce{O}$.
Give it with no units: it is a relative mass.

blocks.question: The relative atomic mass of magnesium is $24.31$. Explain why this value has no units.
steps: Marking point 1: say what the value is compared with, one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Marking point 2: a mass divided by a mass is a ratio, so the units cancel.
Interpret the number in words to show you understand the scale.
blocks.answer: Relative atomic mass compares the mean mass of an atom with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It is a ratio of two masses. The units cancel, so the value has no units. A magnesium atom is on average $24.31$ times heavier than one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.

verify.truth: a ratio of the atom's mass to one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom, so the units cancel

blocks.text: Writing units on $A_\text{r}$ or $M_\text{r}$, such as "$M_\text{r} = \pu{44.01 g}$". Relative masses are plain numbers.

blocks.prompt: What is the relative formula mass of iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate, $\ce{FeSO4.7H2O}$?
blocks.hint: Work out $\ce{FeSO4}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ separately, then add seven waters.
blocks.explain: $\ce{FeSO4}$: $55.85 + 32.07 + 4(16.00) = 151.92$. Seven waters: $7 \times 18.02 = 126.14$. Total $278.06$. $169.94$ adds only one water, $151.92$ leaves the water out, and $1189.58$ multiplies the whole formula by 7.

blocks.prompt: Which statement about carbon dioxide, $\ce{CO2}$, is correct?
blocks.hint: Count both oxygen atoms, and think about whether a relative mass has units.

options.text: Its relative formula mass is 44.01, with no units.
Its relative formula mass is 44.01 g.
Its relative formula mass is 44.01 g mol⁻¹.
Its relative formula mass is 28.01, with no units.

blocks.explain: $M_\text{r} = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01$, and relative masses have no units. The unit $\pu{g mol-1}$ belongs to the molar mass, $M$. $28.01$ counts only one oxygen atom.

verify.truth: Its relative formula mass is 44.01, with no units.

blocks.text: The size of the mole was chosen so the two scales line up. One mole of carbon-12 atoms has a mass of 12 g, correct to better than one part in a billion.
So one mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to its $M_\text{r}$. One mole of water molecules is $\pu{18.02 g}$, a little more than a tablespoon.

blocks.statement: $M$: the mass of one mole of a substance, in $\pu{g mol-1}$. It has the same value as $M_\text{r}$, or $A_\text{r}$ for atoms.
blocks.plain: How many grams one mole weighs.

blocks.text: So $M_\text{r}(\ce{H2O}) = 18.02$ with no units, but $M(\ce{H2O}) = \pu{18.02 g mol-1}$. Same number, different quantity: always give $M$ its units.
This is in section 1 of the data booklet. Use $m$ in grams, $M$ in $\pu{g mol-1}$, and you get $n$ in mol. Rearranged, $m = nM$ and $M = \frac{m}{n}$.

blocks.alt: Three boxes in a row. Left: mass, m, in grams. Middle: amount, n, in moles. Right: number of particles, N. An arrow from mass to amount is labelled divide by M; an arrow back from amount to mass is labelled multiply by M. An arrow from amount to particles is labelled multiply by N A; an arrow back from particles to amount is labelled divide by N A.
blocks.caption: Every route between mass and particles goes through moles.

blocks.question: Calculate the amount, in mol, of urea, $\ce{CO(NH2)2}$, in $\pu{4.50 g}$ of the solid.
steps: Molar mass, from the $A_\text{r}$ values in section 7: one C, one O, two N and four H. $M = 12.01 + 16.00 + 2(14.01) + 4(1.01) = \pu{60.07 g mol-1}$.
Substitute into $n = \frac{m}{M}$: $n = \frac{4.50}{60.07} = 0.074912\ldots$
Round to 3 significant figures, matching $\pu{4.50 g}$, and give the unit.

blocks.question: A tablet contains $\pu{0.325 g}$ of aspirin, $\ce{C9H8O4}$. Determine the number of aspirin molecules in the tablet.
steps: Amount: $n = \frac{0.325}{180.17} = \pu{1.8039e-3 mol}$. Keep this value in your calculator.
Molecules: $N = n \times N_\text{A} = 1.8039 \times 10^{-3} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.0859 \times 10^{21}$.
Round only now, to 3 significant figures.

blocks.text: In a multi-step calculation, carry the unrounded value forward and round only the final answer. Rounding $n$ early can change the last figure and cost the mark.

blocks.prompt: What is the mass, in g, of $\pu{0.0400 mol}$ of sodium carbonate, $\ce{Na2CO3}$? Give 3 significant figures.
What is the mass of one gold atom? Use $A_\text{r}(\ce{Au}) = 196.97$ from the data booklet.
blocks.hint: One mole of gold atoms has a mass of $\pu{196.97 g}$. Share that between $N_\text{A}$ atoms.
blocks.explain: Mass of one atom $= \frac{M}{N_\text{A}} = \frac{196.97}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \approx \pu{3.27e-22 g}$. Multiplying instead gives the huge value, $\frac{N_\text{A}}{M}$ gives the third, and $\pu{197 g}$ is the mass of a whole mole.

blocks.text: Amount of substance, $n$, is counted in moles. A mole of anything holds $N_\text{A}$ elementary entities, about $6.02 \times 10^{23}$: always say which entity.
$A_\text{r}$ and $M_\text{r}$ compare masses with one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom, so they have no units. $M_\text{r}$ is the sum of the $A_\text{r}$ values in the formula.
Molar mass $M$ has the same number as $M_\text{r}$, in $\pu{g mol-1}$.

mistakes: Giving $A_\text{r}$ or $M_\text{r}$ a unit. They are ratios with no units; only the molar mass $M$ has $\pu{g mol-1}$.
Forgetting how many of a particle one formula holds: $\pu{1 mol}$ of $\ce{CaCl2}$ contains $\pu{2 mol}$ of $\ce{Cl^-}$ ions and $\pu{3 mol}$ of ions in all.
Using a mass number, such as 35 for chlorine, instead of the data booklet's $A_\text{r}$ of $35.45$.
Applying a bracket's number to only the last atom: $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$ has two oxygen and two hydrogen atoms.
Dividing the wrong way round. Check the units: $\pu{g} \div \pu{g mol-1}$ gives $\pu{mol}$, so $n = \frac{m}{M}$.
examTips: "Calculate" on Paper 2: write $n = \frac{m}{M}$ with the numbers substituted, then the answer to 3 significant figures with its unit. A correct final answer usually earns full marks, but the working rescues marks after a slip.
Use the data booklet's $A_\text{r}$ values to two decimal places (section 7). Rounded values such as $35.5$ for chlorine can change the final figure.
In Paper 1A, count the particles per formula unit before you look at the options. The wrong options are usually built from skipping that step.
"State" the units of molar mass as $\pu{g mol-1}$, and write $A_\text{r}$ and $M_\text{r}$ as plain numbers.
